messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun is a 53-year-old South Asian man who came to the United States from a region that experienced prolonged civil conflict, and it is that conflict — not the immigration itself — that has quietly dismantled the life he spent decades trying to build. He works as a painter, a trade he has practiced for over twenty years, and until recently it was the thing that most defined him: the physical competence of it, the reliable transformation of a surface, the satisfaction of a finished wall. He is married, and his wife describes him as a man who used to be present. He sought help, he said at intake, because he could no longer pretend the problem was manageable.

The event that anchors everything occurred several years ago, when Arjun was visiting family in his home country. A marketplace explosion — sudden, without warning — killed several people within meters of where he was standing. He was not physically injured, but the sensory world of that moment — the pressure wave moving through his chest, the acrid chemical smell of burning debris, the absolute collapse of any sense that he could protect himself or the people around him — imprinted itself in a way that has not released him. It is that specific loss of control, that moment when the world simply stopped obeying any logic he understood, that lives inside him still.

Back in the United States, the triggers found him before he understood what was happening. On a job site one morning, a contractor slammed a dumpster lid and Arjun dropped to a crouch before he had consciously registered the sound. His body had already decided. He described standing up afterward, hands trembling, certain that every worker on the site had seen him — and that what they saw confirmed something he was beginning to fear about himself: that he was no longer capable of being the man he had been. Ordinary sounds — a car backfiring, a nail gun, a door banging in the wind — now reliably catapult him into a state of full physiological alert, his body tense and scanning, heart elevated, unable to return to baseline for the better part of an hour. This hypervigilance is not merely uncomfortable; it is exhausting in a way that has begun to affect the quality of his work, his concentration, his ability to finish a room cleanly.

The smell of burning — encountered sometimes when clients have fireplaces, or when he passes a construction site with torched materials — carries him back with a completeness that is almost physical. He described the sensation of his body assuming the posture of that marketplace: crouched slightly, arms raised, as though the impact is still arriving. The memory itself feels so extreme, so outside the register of ordinary experience, that he sometimes finds it difficult to believe it belongs to him — and yet it also arrives with overwhelming grief, a grief that is not only for the people who died that day but for the version of himself that existed before it. He has come to believe that the world is genuinely dangerous in a way he simply failed to understand before, and that this knowledge, once acquired, cannot be undone. Nothing feels meaningful in the way it once did; the work that used to ground him now feels like motion without purpose.

These appraisals — that he is diminished, that the world is unsafe, that meaning has drained out of ordinary life — drive the strategies he has assembled to stay functional. He works long hours deliberately, filling every available hour with physical tasks, because stillness allows the memories to surface. He avoids any news coverage of conflict or bombings, knowing that even a headline photograph can trigger an afternoon of intrusion. He goes over and over in his mind why this happened to him specifically — a rumination that promises resolution and delivers none, but that he cannot stop, as though the right answer would somehow metabolize the grief. Yet the busyness, the avoidance, the rumination all circle back: the hypervigilance stays elevated, the body remains primed, and the next trigger — a smell, a sound, a moment of helplessness — finds him no less vulnerable than the last time. His wife has noticed that he flinches at sounds she cannot hear. He has noticed that she has stopped asking him how he is. What he is most afraid of, he said quietly at the end of the first session, is that this is simply who he is now.
